questions.question: Young women who painted glowing numbers on watch dials in New Jersey and Illinois, from about 1917, were taught to shape their brushes to a fine point with their lips, and were told the radium paint was harmless. With every lick the women swallowed a trace of radium. Years later the radium was still inside them, giving off radiation. Why had their bodies kept it?
questions.answer: They built it into bone, as they do calcium
choices: They built it into bone, as they do calcium
They built it into red blood cells, as they do iron
They gathered it in the thyroid, as they do iodine
They stored it in body fat, as they do some vitamins
questions.context: Radium sits in the same column of the periodic table as calcium, and the body handles the two alike, laying radium down in bone, where its alpha particles strike the living cells nearby year after year; radium-226 takes about 1,600 years to decay by half. That is why painters fell ill long after they had left the work. The thyroid does gather iodine and iron does go into red blood cells, but radium follows calcium.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches that the elements in one group of the periodic table share properties (TEKS 2017 8.5C); radium follows its group-mate calcium into bone.

questions.question: Arthur Roeder, president of the United States Radium Corporation, asked Cecil Drinker of the Harvard School of Public Health to study the company's dial-painting plant in New Jersey. Drinker found the plant saturated with radium dust, and his report judged that radium was making the women ill. Roeder insisted that an infection caught outside the factory was to blame. What did the company send New Jersey's Department of Labor?
questions.answer: Drinker's report, changed to say all were well
choices: Drinker's report, changed to say all were well
Drinker's report, just as he had written it
Drinker's report, changed to blame an infection
Nothing, for Roeder kept the report back
questions.context: Alice Hamilton, a Harvard expert on poisons at work, learned that the state's copy said 'every girl is in perfect condition', and in 1925 she asked Katherine Drinker whether Roeder could have issued 'a forged report in your name'. The Drinkers then published their real findings, though Roeder had threatened to sue and had never shown them the company report he said refuted them.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); Drinker's study is evidence that a company was handed and altered.

questions.question: Grace Fryer and four other New Jersey dial painters won a settlement from the United States Radium Corporation in 1928, and Catherine Donohue won her case against the Radium Dial Company in Illinois in 1938. Robley Evans, a physicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, studied former dial painters in the 1930s. A committee he chaired set the first 'tolerance level' for radium workers in 1941. What did it cap?
questions.answer: The radium held in a worker's body
choices: The radium held in a worker's body
The radium a worker handled each day
The radium in each pot of dial paint
The radium on each finished dial
questions.context: The level was 0.1 microgram of radium fixed in the body, a speck too small to see: Evans judged from the painters' cases that no bone cancers would arise below it, and a breath test for radon, the gas radium gives off as it decays, could check a living worker. During the Second World War the Manhattan Project's doctors set their first limit for plutonium in a worker's body by comparing plutonium with radium, and patterned their safety rules on a radium dial plant.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); the painters' cases gave the first safety limit for work with radioactive matter.

questions.question: Chemie Grünenthal began selling thalidomide as a sleeping pill in West Germany in 1957, at first with no prescription needed, and its advertising called the drug non-toxic. On what evidence did the company rest that claim?
questions.answer: Rats and mice had survived huge doses
choices: Rats and mice had survived huge doses
Monkeys given it for months stayed well
Pregnant animals given it had healthy young
Many pregnant women had taken it safely
questions.context: Grünenthal's rodent tests found no dose that would kill, and tests on rodents alone were usual at the time. No pregnant animals were tested and the drug was never tried in pregnant women, though doctors gave it for morning sickness, and rats and mice later proved far less sensitive than rabbits and some monkeys to its harm to unborn young. Late in 1961 Widukind Lenz and William McBride linked it to babies born with shortened or missing limbs, and Grünenthal withdrew it.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to society and the process of science (TEKS 2021 8.4A); a test that found no deaths did not show the drug was safe.

questions.question: Frances Kelsey joined the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August 1960, and one of her first files was Richardson-Merrell's application to sell thalidomide in America. She refused to approve it, month after month, while the company pressed her. What was her objection when she first sent it back, in November 1960?
questions.answer: It had not been shown to be safe
choices: It had not been shown to be safe
It had already harmed babies in Europe
It had killed patients who took too many
It had failed to help patients sleep
questions.context: Kelsey judged that the file leaned on doctors' praise in place of clinical data, with shaky figures on how the body absorbs the drug and unfinished animal studies, and she insisted on hard evidence of safety. She knew of no harm to babies: that link was found in Europe about a year later. Under the law of the day she could turn a drug down only by proving it unsafe, so she asked again and again for more.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to society and the process of science (TEKS 2021 8.4A); Kelsey's demand for evidence of safety is the method at work.

questions.question: Frances Kelsey was still holding back thalidomide at the US Food and Drug Administration when she read a letter in the British Medical Journal from a doctor, A. Leslie Florence. Four of his patients who had taken the sleeping pill nightly for over a year had numbness and tingling in their hands and feet, signs of nerve damage. What did the letter lead Kelsey to ask the company for?
questions.answer: Proof it was safe for unborn babies
choices: Proof it was safe for unborn babies
Proof it worked better than older pills
Proof it was not habit-forming
Proof it did no harm to the liver
questions.context: Nerve damage was not what Kelsey expected of a simple sleeping pill, and the letter led her to ask for proof, animal studies among it, that the drug would not harm a baby before birth; the company's claim that it did not reach the unborn had no support. In May 1961 she wrote to the company that 'the burden of proof that the drug is safe' lay with the applicant. Richardson-Merrell withdrew its application in March 1962, after the birth defects came to light in Europe.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to society and the process of science (TEKS 2021 8.4A); Kelsey followed up an odd side effect instead of ignoring it (map line G8.M3).

questions.question: Frances Kelsey had worked under a law of 1938 that asked a drug company to show only that a new drug was safe. Once thalidomide's harm in Europe came to light, Congress passed the Kefauver-Harris Amendments in October 1962, which added a second thing a company must show before it sells a new drug. What was it?
questions.answer: Evidence from careful studies that it works
choices: Evidence from careful studies that it works
Evidence that it works better than older drugs
Evidence that another country had approved it
Evidence that it costs no more than older drugs
questions.context: The law asks for 'substantial evidence' of the effect a drug claims, drawn from 'adequate and well-controlled investigations', not doctors' praise; it does not ask that a drug beat older ones. It also required that patients in drug trials give informed consent and that makers report side effects. The economist Sam Peltzman argued in 1973 that the new rules also sharply cut the number of new drugs reaching patients each year, a cost the law's defenders weigh against the harms it prevents.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to society, including cost-benefit analysis (TEKS 2021 8.4A); the 1962 law made evidence that a drug works a condition of sale.

questions.question: Doctors of the US Public Health Service began a study in Macon County, Alabama, in 1932 with about 600 Black men: about 400 had syphilis, and about 200 did not. The men were told they were being treated for 'bad blood', a local term for many ills, and were given free medical exams and hot meals. What did the doctors set out to learn?
questions.answer: What syphilis does if it is never treated
choices: What syphilis does if it is never treated
Whether a new drug could cure syphilis
Whether men given syphilis would get well again
Whether a vaccine could prevent syphilis
questions.context: The Public Health Service meant to record the natural course of syphilis left untreated, following the men for the rest of their lives. Its doctors argued that the knowledge would help fight the disease, at a time when the treatments, compounds of arsenic and mercury, were toxic and only mildly effective; but the men were never told they had syphilis and never asked for their informed consent. The doctors did not give anyone the disease: the 399 already had it when they were enrolled.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); the study is the classic case for why research on people needs consent.

questions.question: Penicillin had become the standard cure for syphilis by the late 1940s. The US Public Health Service study in Macon County, Alabama, still followed hundreds of men who had the disease. What did the study's doctors do about the new cure?
questions.answer: They did not offer it to the men
choices: They did not offer it to the men
They gave it to every man who had syphilis
They gave it to half the sick men, to compare
They offered it, but most of the men refused
questions.context: The men were not offered penicillin, and the Public Health Service had already worked to keep them from treatment elsewhere, giving local doctors lists of the men in 1934 and keeping them from treatment when they were drafted in the Second World War. The study was no secret: its doctors published reports on the men in medical journals for decades. Dozens of the men died of syphilis or its effects, and some of their wives and children caught it.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); the cure withheld is the turning point of the Tuskegee record.

questions.question: Peter Buxtun, who interviewed patients with venereal diseases for the US Public Health Service in San Francisco, protested its Alabama syphilis study to his superiors in 1966 and again in 1968. A committee at the federal Center for Disease Control reviewed the study in 1969 and let it go on. What brought the study to an end in 1972?
questions.answer: A news story that made it public
choices: A news story that made it public
A court order won by the men's lawyers
A new law passed by the US Congress
The death of the last man in the study
questions.context: The 1969 committee saw a unique chance to study late syphilis. Buxtun then passed the story to Jean Heller of the Associated Press, whose report ran on 25 July 1972, and an advisory panel judged the study 'ethically unjustified'; it was ended on 16 November 1972, with 74 of the men still alive. The men's lawsuit and the new law for research came afterwards.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); Buxtun's years of protest are dissent inside an institution.

questions.question: Congress passed the National Research Act in 1974, after the US Public Health Service's study of syphilis in Alabama came to light. Under the federal rules that grew from it, nearly all research on people that the US government pays for needs approval before it begins. What must approve it?
questions.answer: A review board that weighs its ethics
choices: A review board that weighs its ethics
The Surgeon General of the United States
A judge of a federal court
The scientists' own professional society
questions.context: Each institution doing such research keeps an institutional review board (IRB), with members from outside science, which weighs the risks to the people in a study and checks that each gives informed consent: told the truth, understanding it, and free to say no. The commission the act set up wrote the Belmont Report in 1979, whose principles are respect for persons, beneficence and justice.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade relates past research to its impact on society (TEKS 2021 8.4A); society, not science, decided the rules for research on people (map line G8.M3).
